Translations.Title: Functions and Function Notation
Translations.Explanation:
Learning objectives: distinguish a function from a relation; evaluate values and equations using function notation; decide when a function is one-to-one; use vertical and horizontal line tests; and identify basic toolkit families and their domains.

Begin by listing ordered pairs and discussing the independent and dependent variables. Have learners test whether repeated inputs produce conflicting outputs. A repeated output alone does not violate the definition of a function.

Represent input-output rules with f(x). Interpret real-world input labels and numeric inputs, and make substitutions including x=−2, a and a+h. When solving f(x)=c, seek all permitted input values rather than evaluating f(c).

Compare tables, formulas and plotted points. Use vertical lines to test single-valuedness and horizontal lines to test whether the function is one-to-one. For implicit curves, inspect upper and lower branches separately.

Use graphical and tabular toolkit-family tasks: linear, square, cube, absolute-value, reciprocal, square-root, constant and identity. Record domain restrictions such as x≠0 for 1/x and x≥0 for √x.

Teacher-led activity: provide coordinate grids or a graphing tool. Ask learners to draw y=x², x=y² and y=|x|−1, sketch vertical and horizontal test lines, annotate all intersections, and justify results orally or in writing. Teacher validates hand-drawn scale and mathematical claims; these are not automatically scored.

Independent section practice can include verbal descriptions, algebraic relations, tables, graph classification, technology-assisted view windows and applied situations. Independent exercises, including table, algebra, graph, and applied tasks, must be discussed using their own models, units and stated input domains. A teacher checks graph drawings and written explanations.

Teacher checkpoint: compare an input/output mapping, a function evaluation, an inverse-direction ambiguity and two graph tests. Keep contextual units visible. Alternate representations must preserve the definition and intended domain; graph accuracy is a human review task until the display contract is exercised.

Independent Try It 1 — Classifying a pair of mappings. In a small library, book IDs A, B, C identify titles Alpha, Beta, Gamma without duplicates. Is title a function of book ID? Is book ID a function of title? Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 2 — Function notation in context. A plant's measured height h in centimetres depends on the day d since planting. Express this as a named function and state what h(8)=17 means. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 3 — Classification of a table. A table contains input/output pairs (1,10), (2,100), (3,1000). Decide whether this is a function and justify. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 4 — Evaluate an integer radical. For f(t)=sqrt(t-9), calculate f(13) and state the real domain. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 5 — Solve an integer radical equation. For f(t)=sqrt(t-9), find the input with output four. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 6 — Isolate a cubed dependent variable. Rewrite x=27y^3 as y=f(x) for real x. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 7 — Evaluate a table-encoded function. The table shows (0,6), (1,8), (2,10). Find g(1). Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 8 — Solve a function equation from a graph. On coordinate paper, graph f(x)=|x-1|, then identify each x at which f(x)=1. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 9 — Inverse direction in a contextual mapping. Each employee is assigned exactly one department, and at least two employees are assigned to the same department. Is department a function of employee? Is employee a function of department? Is the first function one-to-one? Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 10 — Contextual function versus injectivity. A score from 0 to 100 determines exactly one letter grade, and several scores share each letter. Is letter grade a function of numeric score? Is it one-to-one? Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 11 — Vertical-line test for a graph. Sketch y=|x| and explain whether each vertical line meets its graph in at most one point. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Independent Try It 12 — Horizontal-line test for a function. Graph y=x^2 on all real inputs. Is it one-to-one? Provide a horizontal-line counterexample. Explain your reasoning to your teacher; diagrams and open-ended reasoning are teacher-reviewed.

Instructor-graded graphical practice (source Section 1.1, exercises 52–59): learners read labelled axes, distinguish a graph that fails the vertical-line test from one that merely fails one-to-one, and justify every horizontal-line intersection. An original source graph beginning near (−2,0) shows f(−1)≈1; its displayed right-hand curve does not establish an exact input for f(x)=3, so students must label any extrapolated value as an estimate. Follow the separate teacher rubric; these diagrams and explanations have no proven automatic grader or production delivery.

Edulytics cool-down: given R={(1,2),(1,4),(2,4)}, classify R and explain; evaluate f(−1) for f(x)=x²−2x+1; and decide whether h(x)=x² is one-to-one when x≥0. Submit reasons. A teacher reviews the explanation; this cool-down is independently authored, not a reproduction of teacher-restricted material.

First-party supplemental example — overlapping horizontal-ray domains. For y=3 when x>0 and y=−3 when x<2, the two rules overlap for 0<x<2. At x=1 the relation contains both (1,3) and (1,−3); it fails the vertical-line test. Explain this with labelled axes. This is an Edulytics original illustration, not the original publisher graphic.

First-party table for worked example 11: x inputs −1, 0, 1, 2 correspond respectively to f(x) values 4, 1, 4, 9. Read f(0)=1. To solve f(x)=4 from the table, report both displayed inputs, x=−1 and x=1. The table alone cannot determine outputs for unlisted inputs.

Tables for Section 1.1: each input can have exactly one output while several distinct inputs may share a result. The 14 first-party source-skill table representations include menu/grade interpretation, nonnumeric inputs, tabulated function tests, month/day values, lookup and inverted lookup, basic toolkit families, and the Section exercise table. Inspect all original axes, figure captions and source table numerals separately when grading original exercises.

Notation choice — in applied mathematics one may write y=y(x). For introductory function analysis, y=f(x) distinguishes the function rule f from the output value y, so treat them as different mathematical roles.

Implicit function subtlety — an equation can determine one output for each input without giving an easy explicit formula for that output. Test uniqueness of the output branch; conversely, equations such as a circle may produce two real y-values for the same x and are not functions of x.

Function notation uses parentheses to indicate the INPUT to a function, not multiplication: f(a+b) applies f after determining a+b as one complete input.

A table can list every known pair or selected observations from a wider relationship. A few sampled ordered pairs do not determine how the function behaves outside the table.

A graph may consist of isolated plotted values for a discrete domain, or the complete curve representing all ordered pairs in a continuous domain. Plotting sampled points alone does not prove continuity between them.

The nine basic toolkit-function families are constant, identity, absolute value, quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, reciprocal squared, square root, and cube root. For reciprocal and reciprocal squared exclude x=0; the square root has real x>=0.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules:
Relation, domain and range: A relation is a set of ordered input-output pairs; its domain contains inputs and its range contains outputs.
Rule: An x or other input can occur more than once, but a function forbids conflicting outputs for that input.
Example: {(1,2),(2,4),(2,4)} is a function.

Definition of a function: Each allowed input is assigned exactly one output.
Rule: To disprove a function, exhibit an input paired with two distinct outputs.
Example: {(1,2),(1,3)} is not a function.

Function notation and dependent quantity: f(x) names the output produced by f on input x; inputs can be labels as well as numbers.
Rule: Evaluate f(a) by substituting a for every occurrence of the input.
Example: f(x)=x²+1 gives f(−2)=5.

Evaluating a function expression: An input such as a+h must be treated as one substituted object.
Rule: For f(x)=x², f(a+h)=(a+h)²=a²+2ah+h², not a²+h².
Example: f(x)=x²+3x−4 implies [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h=2a+h+3 when h≠0.

Solving for an input: Solving f(x)=c asks which input values yield output c.
Rule: Set the function expression equal to c and solve, testing domain restrictions.
Example: p²+2p=3 yields p=1 or p=−3.

One-to-one (injective): A function is one-to-one when different inputs never have the same output.
Rule: f(a)=f(b) implies a=b, with the specified domain.
Example: r↦πr² is one-to-one for r≥0.

Vertical and horizontal graph tests: Vertical-line intersections test whether y is a function of x; horizontal-line intersections test one-to-one.
Rule: No vertical line may meet a function graph twice; no horizontal line may meet a one-to-one function graph twice.
Example: y=x² passes vertical but fails horizontal.

Basic function families: Toolkit graphs include constant, identity, square, cube, absolute value, reciprocal, square root and related transformations.
Rule: Graph shape, domain and function notation must be understood together; reciprocal excludes x=0 and square root requires x≥0.
Example: f(x)=1/x is undefined at 0; g(x)=√x is real for x≥0.

Basic toolkit function families: Nine toolkit families: constant, identity, absolute value, quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, reciprocal squared, square root, and cube root. Read formula, graph, domain and range together: 1/x and 1/x² exclude x=0, while √x requires x≥0.
Translations.WorkedExamples:
1. Can an item determine its price?
Task: A ticket desk sells adult tickets for $12, student tickets for $8, and senior tickets for $8. Is ticket price a function of ticket category? Is category a function of price?
Method: Check whether each input is associated with exactly one output.
Step 1: For category-to-price, each of adult, student and senior has exactly one displayed dollar amount.
Step 2: For price-to-category, the $8 input corresponds to two categories: student and senior.
Step 3: Therefore category-to-price is a function, while price-to-category is not.
Answer: Price is a function of category; category is not a function of price.
Check: Repeated output values are allowed for a function; repeated inputs with distinct outputs are not.

2. Classify a grade-band rule
Task: Suppose percentages 78–86 map to GPA 3.0 and 87–91 map to GPA 3.5. Is GPA a function of percentage? Is percentage a function of GPA?
Method: Treat the input-to-output rule as a mapping, not an average.
Step 1: Every percentage in the specified bands has one GPA according to the table.
Step 2: Many percentages, such as 80 and 85, both map to GPA 3.0.
Step 3: Thus GPA depends functionally on percentage, while reversing the direction is not single-valued.
Answer: GPA is a function of percentage; percentage is not a function of GPA.
Check: For the inverse direction, GPA 3.0 has more than one possible percentage.

3. Express a nonnumeric input in function notation
Task: The number of scheduled stops depends on the bus route. Route A has 7 stops and route B has 12. Express these facts using function notation.
Method: Identify the independent variable before naming the function.
Step 1: Take the route label as input r and its number of stops as output.
Step 2: Define s(r) as the number of stops assigned to route r.
Step 3: Evaluate at the named routes.
Answer: s(A)=7 and s(B)=12.
Check: The input is a route label; it does not need to be a number.

4. Interpret a function-value statement
Task: Let N(y) be the number of employees of a company in year y. Explain N(2024)=135.
Method: Read the input and output in context.
Step 1: Identify 2024 as the input year.
Step 2: Identify N(y) as a headcount rather than a year or dollar amount.
Step 3: State the observation using the correct units.
Answer: In 2024 the company employed 135 people.
Check: Do not confuse the input year with the output headcount.

5. Determine whether a table is a function
Task: Compare three independently authored relation tables. Table A: (2,1),(5,3),(8,6). Table B: (-3,5),(0,1),(4,5). Table C: (1,0),(5,2),(5,4). Classify whether EACH table defines y as a function of x; for the functional tables decide whether one-to-one, with reasons.
Method: Check each input and its output independently in all three tables; then test repeated outputs.
Step 1: Table A has three distinct inputs and three distinct outputs: it is a one-to-one function.
Step 2: Table B has distinct inputs, but -3 and 4 both map to 5: it is a function but not one-to-one.
Step 3: Table C maps the same input 5 to both 2 and 4: it is not a function at all.
Answer: Table A: one-to-one function. Table B: function but not one-to-one. Table C: not a function.
Check: A repeated output is allowed for a function; a repeated input with a conflicting output is not.

6. Evaluate and simplify an input expression
Task: For f(x)=x²+3x−4, calculate f(2), f(a), f(a+h), and [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h for h≠0.
Method: Substitute the entire input before expanding.
Step 1: Evaluate at x=2: f(2)=4+6−4=6.
Step 2: Evaluate at symbolic input a: f(a)=a²+3a−4.
Step 3: At input a+h, f(a+h)=(a+h)²+3(a+h)−4=a²+2ah+h²+3a+3h−4.
Step 4: For h≠0, subtract f(a) from f(a+h), factor h, then simplify the difference quotient to 2a+h+3.
Answer: f(2)=6; f(a)=a²+3a−4; f(a+h)=a²+2ah+h²+3a+3h−4; quotient=2a+h+3.
Check: The quotient expression requires h≠0.

7. Evaluate at a numeric input
Task: Given h(p)=p²+2p, evaluate h(4).
Method: Replace every p with 4 and respect order of operations.
Step 1: Write h(4)=4²+2(4).
Step 2: Calculate 4²=16 and 2(4)=8.
Step 3: Add the terms to obtain 24.
Answer: 24
Check: 16+8=24, not 36.

8. Solve a function-value equation
Task: For h(p)=p²+2p, find all inputs p for which h(p)=3.
Method: Equate the function output to 3 and solve the quadratic.
Step 1: Set p²+2p=3, or p²+2p−3=0.
Step 2: Factor (p+3)(p−1)=0.
Step 3: Check p=−3 and p=1 in h.
Answer: p=−3 or p=1.
Check: h(−3)=9−6=3 and h(1)=1+2=3.

9. Isolate an output variable
Task: Rewrite 2n+6p=12 as p=f(n).
Method: Isolate p using equation-preserving operations.
Step 1: Subtract 2n: 6p=12−2n.
Step 2: Divide all terms by 6: p=(12−2n)/6.
Step 3: Simplify the two terms.
Answer: p=f(n)=2−n/3.
Check: Substituting gives 2n+6(2−n/3)=12.

10. Why the unit circle is not a y-function
Task: Does x²+y²=1 specify one value of y for every x on [−1,1]?
Method: Identify when one x has more than one y.
Step 1: At x=0, the equation becomes y²=1.
Step 2: Both y=1 and y=−1 satisfy the relation.
Step 3: Without a branch restriction, the relation fails to specify a single y value.
Answer: No. The upper branch y=√(1−x²) and lower branch y=−√(1−x²) separately define functions on [−1,1].
Check: The two points (0,1) and (0,−1) have the same input.

11. Read and solve from tabulated values
Task: A table gives f(−1)=4, f(0)=1, f(1)=4, f(2)=9. Evaluate f(0) and find every table input with f(x)=4.
Method: Read values from recorded ordered pairs.
Step 1: Locate x=0 and read its listed output 1.
Step 2: Scan the output column for 4.
Step 3: Report both input values −1 and 1.
Answer: f(0)=1; the listed solutions of f(x)=4 are x=−1 and x=1.
Check: Do not assume these are the only solutions outside the given table.

12. Extract values from a graph description
Task: A plotted V-shaped graph represents f(x)=|x|−1. Find f(−2) and all x with f(x)=2.
Method: Translate the graph to the equivalent absolute-value rule.
Step 1: Read f(−2)=|−2|−1=1.
Step 2: Solve |x|−1=2, giving |x|=3.
Step 3: Use both branches of the absolute value equation.
Answer: f(−2)=1; x=−3 or x=3.
Check: A graph horizontal line y=2 intersects this V shape twice.

13. Area as a one-to-one function of radius
Task: Is the area of a circular disk a function of radius r≥0? Is it one-to-one on this domain?
Method: Use the area formula and the physical domain.
Step 1: Set A(r)=πr² with r≥0.
Step 2: Every nonnegative radius has exactly one area.
Step 3: For nonnegative radii, larger r gives strictly larger area, so equal areas require equal radii.
Answer: Yes, A is a function and is one-to-one for r≥0.
Check: Without r≥0, r and −r would share the same area; domain matters.

14. Apply the vertical-line test
Task: Apply the vertical-line test to three independent model graphs: (A) y=x², (B) y=2x+1, and (C) y²=x. Which of A, B, C represent y as a function of x, and why?
Method: Check whether a vertical line can hit the graph more than once.
Step 1: A: each real x has one output x², so every vertical line meets the parabola at most once.
Step 2: B: each real x has exactly one output 2x+1, so a nonvertical straight line passes.
Step 3: C: at x=4 the sideways relation contains both (4,2) and (4,-2), so it fails.
Answer: Graphs A and B are functions of x. Graph C is not a function of x.
Check: The test concerns the number of outputs for a SINGLE x; it is not a test of injectivity.

15. Apply the horizontal-line test
Task: Compare f(x)=(x−1)² and g(x)=2x−1 on all real inputs. Which functions are one-to-one?
Method: Look for repeated outputs at different x values.
Step 1: f(0)=1 and f(2)=1, so one horizontal line intersects f twice.
Step 2: If g(a)=g(b), then 2a−1=2b−1 forces a=b.
Step 3: Therefore the linear nonconstant g is one-to-one and the parabola f is not.
Answer: g(x)=2x−1 is one-to-one; f(x)=(x−1)² is not.
Check: Restricting f to x≥1 would make it one-to-one, but that is a different domain.

16. Two horizontal rays with overlapping input domains
Task: A relation is formed from two horizontal rays: y=3 when x>0 and y=−3 when x<2. Is the relation y=f(x)? Justify your answer using a vertical line.
Method: Check where the two permitted input domains overlap, rather than treating each ray in isolation.
Step 1: The upper ray includes all x>0, while the lower ray includes all x<2.
Step 2: Both rules apply to every input with 0<x<2.
Step 3: Choose x=1. The relation includes (1,3) and (1,−3), so a vertical line x=1 intersects it twice.
Answer: No. The combined relation is not a function of x: for every x in (0,2) there are two distinct outputs.
Check: Whether a ray has an open endpoint does not matter if the rays' input domains overlap elsewhere.

Translations.CommonMistakes:
Treating a repeated output as evidence that a relation is not a function.
Why incorrect: Many different inputs may lead to one output.
Correction: Check whether any one input has two distinct outputs.

Computing f(a+h) as f(a)+f(h) without justification.
Why incorrect: Functions generally do not distribute across addition of inputs.
Correction: Substitute the full expression a+h into the defining formula.

Answering f(x)=3 by substituting x=3.
Why incorrect: The problem asks for an input that produces output 3, not for f(3).
Correction: Solve the equation f(x)=3 and check the solutions.

Using the horizontal-line test to decide whether a relation is a function.
Why incorrect: Horizontal-line test checks injectivity, not single-valuedness.
Correction: First apply vertical-line test; only then apply horizontal-line test.

Calling a circle graph y=f(x) without a branch restriction.
Why incorrect: A single x can have both positive and negative y solutions.
Correction: Select upper or lower semicircle and state the domain.

Assuming a pair of separate horizontal rays automatically passes the vertical-line test.
Why incorrect: Two separate pieces can give different y-values for the same x if their input domains overlap.
Correction: Write the x-domain of each piece and test their intersection; for the two-ray example any x in (0,2) yields two y-values.
Translations.QuickSummary:
A function assigns exactly one output to every allowed input.
Repeated inputs are permitted only when their outputs agree.
f(x) is the output at input x; f(x)=c asks for possible inputs.
One-to-one means distinct inputs have distinct outputs.
Vertical-line test checks function status; horizontal-line test checks one-to-one status.
Toolkit functions require correct domains, graph shapes and units.
Open-ended graph interpretation and written proof are teacher-reviewed.
Two separate graph pieces can still fail to define a function when their input domains overlap and assign different outputs.
